A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining planetary nebulae with similar spectral properties, particularly those exhibiting [He II] 656er line emission, which can be used to define nebular spectra in the local universe. This method avoids planetary nebulae spectra correction and facilitates independent distance estimates by analyzing the [O III] 5000r line width and mean [O III] 5000r and H-alpha line ratios within planetary nebulae associated with galaxies. A comparative study of this method and traditional techniques to measure the distance to galaxies in the Fornax cluster yielded an average difference of 1.95 kpc, with a standard deviation of 8.09 kpc, and produced comparable results with a coefficient of determination (R-square) of 0.86, indicating a strong correlation between the two distance estimation approaches. Despite individual errors of up to 20 kpc, this method is effective for large galaxy samples, has been automated, and has been applied to galaxies in the Fornax cluster using data from the VLT/MUSE spectrograph as part of the Fornax3D survey. The resulting distance estimates have been made available in a companion paper. The preprocessed planetary nebulae spectra are also available for further analysis. The accuracy of this method is expected to improve with the advent of higher sensitivity spectrographs that can detect fainter planetary nebulae associated with galaxies. The code used to develop this method is publicly available. The Planetary Nebulae Distance Estimator (PANE) code is based on multivariate methods and can be tailored to use different line ratios and width ranges to suit various observational datasets. The current version of PANE code is capable of analyzing planetary nebulae associated with galaxies in the local universe and has been successfully applied to galaxies in the Fornax cluster using data from the VLT/MUSE spectrograph as part of the Fornax3D survey. The code has been developed using the Python programming language and relies on the scikit-learn, scipy, and numpy libraries. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of sensitive patient data through various medical applications, producing data streams that need to be analyzed in real-time. These streams, once processed, are subject to strict confidentiality requirements that must be observed. Unfortunately, existing stream processing systems, designed for efficiency and scalability, do not adequately address the confidentiality concerns surrounding medical data. To address this shortcoming, we present LifeStream, a stream processing engine tailored for (i) real-time data processing, (ii) confidentiality in stream data, and (iii) limited memory. LifeStream supports both continuous and discrete streams and incorporates a rich set of operators, including window operators. We have implemented LifeStream as a Java plugin for Apache Flink and tested it on both synthetic and real medical data, demonstrating its superior performance and efficiency in various scenarios. Across all tests, LifeStream surpassed a base Flink implementation in terms of execution time while maintaining comparable memory usage. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibited superior performance when compared to other stream processing frameworks, such as Apache Spark Streaming and Distributed Flux, across all tests, with a particular advantage observed when using small memory configurations. The underlying principles and performance-driven design of LifeStream also provide valuable insights for developing similar efficient and scalable stream processing engines in various domains beyond healthcare. The source code for LifeStream is available openly on GitHub at https://github.com/ammarub/LifeStream. The evaluation results and additional information can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/streams-at-icde2023/home.

Despite its advantages, the HHL algorithm has significant requirements, including access to large quantities of noisy qubits and precise amplitude amplification, which pose significant challenges for quantum operations on limited numbers of qubits. This paper presents NISQ-HHL, a modified HHL algorithm designed to address these challenges by incorporating additional error correction measures, specifically amplitude amplification and resource management, aimed at optimizing qubit utilization and minimizing operation duration. Furthermore, NISQ-HHL was found to be highly adaptable, with a 4-qubit version demonstrating a 4.3-fold reduction in execution time and a 5.4-fold reduction in error bar. These findings validate the efficacy of the NISQ-HHL portfolio and highlight its potential as a versatile and highly adaptable error correction measure for the HHL algorithm, with applications across a broad spectrum of linear algebraic problems. Given its modular design, it is also possible to modify NISQ-HHL for use with other solvers that employ amplitude amplification, offering a valuable contribution to the field of quantum computing. To enhance speech recognition using state-of-the-art transformers, two issues need to be addressed: incorporating external knowledge from text datasets and minimizing over-reliance on abundant training data. To tackle these challenges, a new speech-text oriented multi-modal training method called bidirectional focus for improved speech recognition (BFFSR) is proposed. This technique employs two distinct streams to process speech and text, with each stream focused on the complementary information. By positioning the cross-modal attention module in the middle of the transformer, BFFSR ensures that the information is processed in both directions, allowing for the exchange of knowledge between speech and text. The proposed model is simple, yet efficient and effective in improving speech recognition performance. Experimental results show that BFFSR achieves significant improvements over conventional training and reduces the over-reliance on abundant data. Moreover, by adjusting the ratio of speech and text streams, BFFSR enables efficient utilization of limited labeled data, resulting in up to 8.32% absolute improvement in correct transcription. The code for BFFSR is publicly available at https://github.com/lingcat/BFFSR.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Although the model assumes a non-relativistic description of quarks, it provides a good fit to calculated masses to the level of 10%, and predicts additional narrow resonance states of the Ω-baryon. A comparison with the approach of the "constarized" Bethe-Salpeter method is also presented, showcasing both methods' results on magnetic moments, form factors, and decay widths. The epitaxial growth of materials on graphene-based substrates offers a game changer by minimizing defects and facilitating the creation of complex multilayer structures. To fully utilize this technology, a a comprehensive understanding of the equilibrium between remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy is crucial. In this study, a comprehensive analysis of the equilibrium between these growth modes was achieved by investigating the epitaxy of Heusler films on graphene/sapphire substrates using in situ methods. A range of techniques including x-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and atomic force microscopy were used to evaluate the film's structure, surface morphology, and orientation. A precise assessment of the surface and orbital moments was also obtained through reciprocal space mapping and x-ray magnetic circular dichroism. A detailed examination of the film's composition, surface morphology, and orientation allowed for the identification of four equilibrium states corresponding to remote, pinhole, van der Waals, and mixed epitaxy. Notably, a clean and defect-free AlGaHeusler layer was found to exhibit remote epitaxy, whereas the addition of oxygen residues switched the equilibrium to pinhole or van der Waals epitaxy. Consequently, this study demonstrates the extraordinary versatility of graphene-based substrates and confirms their capability to accommodate a wide range of growth modes, from remote to van der Waals epitaxy. This is coupled with the observed dependence of the equilibrium state on gas residue, which can be controlled through proper annealing procedures. As such, this research has significant implications for the successful fabrication of complex multilayer Heusler structures, and it also provides a valuable understanding of the growth mechanisms of van der Waals epitaxy on graphene-based substrates. This knowledge can be further utilized to develop a precise control over the epitaxial growth of Heusler films and other materials on graphene/sapphire substrates. This can be achieved by appropriately selecting the substrate temperature, film thickness, and composition to access the desired growth mode, thereby facilitating the creation of multilayer Heusler structures with controlled magnetocrystalline anisotropy and surface roughness. We examine the potential output of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) for a specific type of leptoquark pair production - namely, pairs of different leptoquark types - with the assumption that only two leptoquark pairs exist as fundamental particles. Existing research has demonstrated that in many scenarios, only one leptoquark type would be detectable through LHC data. In contrast, our analysis highlights instances where both leptoquark types could be identified, often with distinct signature patterns, and even situations where the lighter leptoquark remains undetected unless combined with data from a future 100 TeV particle accelerator. In evaluating these possibilities, we consider various particle combinations and illustrate our findings with graphical representations, offering a clear visual understanding of the relevant physical processes. Furthermore, our research utilizes the Hegner and Reichert leptoquark production tool and takes into account various particle properties and potential detection limitations within the LHC. In closing, our analysis highlights the capacity of the LHC to discern both members of a leptoquark duo in specific scenarios, and the importance of searching for these pairs across a wide range of combinations and orientations. We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-induced three-body recombination from spinless dimer states, which can be realized using atom-molecule trapping systems with a 1D configuration. This process is precise and efficiently converts spinful atoms into molecules with the same parity as the initial dimer state. Our calculations demonstrate how varying the wavelength of the breaking laser, as well as the interaction between dimer states and background atoms, affects the efficiency of this process. Additionally, we have examined two scenarios: one where the initial state is a symmetric spinless dimer state, and another where the initial state is an asymmetric spinful dimer state. In both cases, our research shows that it is possible to achieve over 50% efficiency in recombining the dimer into a single molecule. Our study also illustrates how this process can be optimized by adjusting the strength of the interaction between the dimer states and the surrounding atoms, although this is more challenging for asymmetric dimer states. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that in both scenarios, combining the process with cooling techniques leads to even higher efficiency rates. Our research indicates that the lowest possible level of spinful atom-molecule conversion can be achieved within a critical parameter window, which can be minimized by adjusting the ratio of the breaking laser's intensity to its wavelength squared. Our findings also suggest that in both scenarios, it is possible to achieve an average molecule-molecule interaction energy that is several times greater than the temperature of the trapping system. A superdiffusive transport model is often characterized by a mean-square displacement that scales differently than linearly with time, and this behavior can be attributed to various sources including randomness, structural interactions, and fluid properties. In this research, we investigate the fundamental principles of random permeability that contribute to the transport of a tracer within a fractal geometry, and by doing so, we explore the possibility that the transport dynamics can be explained by a constant diffusion coefficient and random efficacy. Specifically, we show that the efficacy can be considered a Markov process, and in several specialized cases, we determine the probability distributions of the efficacy in relation to transport dimensions. Consequently, we derive the general equation that describes the average distance of the tracer from its initial position over time, resulting in the Lagrangian operator that determines the transport dimensions in terms of the efficacy distribution. This operator enables us to classify diffusive scenarios into distinct categories based on the efficacy distribution parameters, and it further implies that the efficacy can switch between different states within a time that is much faster than the time it takes for the tracer to move across the fractal structure. In the limit where the efficacy switches between two states, we obtain the specific transport dimensions, and by extending this to an infinite number of states, we determine the transport dimensions for any arbitrary distribution of efficacy, thereby providing a unified diffusion law that encompasses all scenarios. This diffusion law is validated through numerous random efficacy configurations, and it highlights the significance of considering the efficacy distribution in transport dimensions, and the sole reliance on the average diffusion coefficient is insufficient. A transition from an inside-out to a outside-in star formation slowdown has been observed in galaxies. While this behavior may be linked to the evolution of bulge and disk components, it's necessary to consider interactions with the surrounding environment and mass assemblies. Using a comprehensive dataset including optical, infrared, and radio data for nearly 3000 galaxies within 0.02 steradians of the sky, we analyzed the motiving factors behind the turn-over of the M*-SFR relation by examining the galaxy population in the Coma region and throughout the whole sky. Galaxies in the Coma region exhibit a similar relation to more distant galaxies with the same optical brightness, indicating that the relation isn't significantly affected by the environment. A separation of the bulge and disk star formation components reveals that the slowdown in the center of galaxies may post-date the slowdown on the outside. This suggests that the threshold mass where the relation turns over might depend on the bulge-to-total mass ratio rather than being constant. Furthermore, this interpretation is consistent with the relation's behavior in the whole sky, where the B/T ratio varies greatly. Therefore, we propose that the turn-over mass where the relation turns over could be approximately 10 times the bulge mass, which may also be linked to the threshold mass where quenching begins. The turn-over mass where the relation turns over could also be influenced by the presence of massive bulges in massive elliptical galaxies, which may be quenching quickly due to their lack of star forming material. X-ray images contain rich information that can be used to determine the characteristics of COVID-19 patients admitted to the ICU.  To investigate this, a dataset of X-ray images was collected, both from patients with mild, moderate, and severe symptoms, as well as those who required ICU care.  A distinction was made between the images based on symptoms, without consideration of the patients' ICU status, and on the patients' ICU status alone.  A machine learning model was trained to differentiate between these groups and provide important features, which were then analyzed to determine the ICU admission criteria they imply.  Our results show that the following characteristics are indicative of ICU admission: the presence of vertical lines indicating blood vessel damage, circular patterns representing lung abscesses, and the distribution of opacities in the upper lobes.  It is essential to note that ICU admission decisions are complex and multifaceted, and these findings are not a substitute for medical expertise but rather a supplementary tool to aid in this process.  Moreover, a discussion is presented on possible future improvements, including the integration of clinical data with the image analysis, and the use of transfer learning to enhance the accuracy of the model.  This research can be applicable to other respiratory diseases characterized by lung opacities.  Finally, the code and dataset used in this study are available online, as mentioned in the appendix.  It is crucial to note that this work does not aim to replace medical professionals but rather to provide a supplementary tool to aid in the assessment of ICU admission for patients based on X-ray images, as well as to provide an example of how machine learning can be applied to this problem.  The code and dataset used in this study are available online, as mentioned in the appendix.  It is also worth mentioning that this research can be applicable to other respiratory diseases characterized by lung opacities. This paper delves into the source of high precise, yet low-focused results in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). Precisely, it investigates why precise VRD models tend to incorrectly assign relationships to a large number of individual elements within an image. To achieve this, it compares the unique challenges of VRD with other object-based detection tasks. Differentiating VRD from other object-based detection tasks like Open-Vocabulary Object Detection, it identifies two distinct challenges. First, VRD involves discovering multiple types of relationships across an image, making it harder to establish a reliable connection between objects. Second, it requires relationship annotations that span an infinite number of possible descriptions, presenting a labeling difficulty. To overcome these challenges, it proposes a multi-stage approach that addresses the challenges of VRD in the training and inference processes. During training, it limits the number of relationships discovered for a given image. During inference, it refines the predictions by eliminating erroneous positive relationships between objects. To further enhance the focus of VRD models, it introduces a simple yet effective thresholding technique. To support our method's effectiveness, it presents experimental results showing the proposed approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art in focused VRD evaluation metrics. Moreover, it demonstrates that the proposed approach's performance in general VRD evaluation metrics remains highly competitive. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/zwang84/Focused-VRD.

A key distinction between NGCPs and conventional Golay complementary pairs (GCPs) is that the elements of an NGCP belong to different sequence lengths. Moreover, a method for creating pairs of GCSs from GCPs is introduced and utilized to generate a 2-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4 and 6. A 4-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8 is also designed using the NGCP framework, although it cannot be achieved using traditional GCP design. A numerical optimization is performed to enhance the orthogonality of one 4-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8. A 6-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8 is also proposed and discussed. A 4-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, as well as a 6-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, can be further optimized by applying a convolution method to their elements, which in turn enhances their autocorrelation properties. A corresponding receiver algorithm is also provided. A comparison is conducted between our proposed 4-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, a 4-phase Golay complementary set with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, and a 4-phase ZComplementary Code (ZCC) with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, in terms of their autocorrelation properties. A spreading sequence design based on NGCP can be applied to support multiple users, and a numerical example is provided to illustrate this concept. A hardware-implementable receiver algorithm is proposed and a corresponding simulation environment is created to simulate and evaluate the performance of our proposed 4-phase PGCS with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, a 4-phase ZCC with sequences of lengths 4, 6, and 8, and a 4-phase Golay complementary set with sequences of lengths 4

Quantum interactions between valleys in silicon have long been recognized, and researchers believe they could be utilized for efficient data processing.  However, due pressure and temperature variations, the valley interaction changes, making it necessary to examine their effects on silicon's electronic properties.  This study used atomic scale tunneling to investigate silicon's nanoscale behavior within the 50valley interaction range, revealing that the temperature dependence of valley interaction is directly related to spin transfer, and that their combination creates complex patterns influencing the silicon's electronic structure.  Additionally, we discovered pressure-induced valence band modifications and the presence of Dirac cones in silicon, driven by its unique crystal structure.  These findings demonstrate the intricate interconnections between silicon's electronic properties, its atomic and crystalline composition, and how they are impacted by applied pressure and temperature.  As this study used experimental valley marking with 60electron beams, it also explores the potential of silicon's valley structure and spin interactions for reliable and efficient data processing systems.  Moreover, we propose a device concept based on silicon's unique valley and spin interactions, which could be used to create fast and reliable memory storage components called spin-OR RAM.  These breakthrough discoveries and proposed applications prove that silicon's complexity is also its strength, and it possesses a level of sophistication that could be adapted and harnessed for a wide range of data processing purposes.  This research was conducted by examining silicon nanowires, nanoslices, and layered silicon crystals, and it provides a comprehensive understanding of the valley structure, spin interactions, and atomic composition that makes silicon so complex, as well as the various effects that pressure and temperature have on its electronic structure.  This knowledge could be utilized to enhance existing silicon-based technology, and it also provides a foundation for developing a range of innovative applications based on silicon's unique valley and spin structures.  In addition, we have made a silicon valley marking simulator that is available online, and it allows users to examine the effects of different conditions on silicon's valley structure and spin interactions, and to adapt this technology for a wide range of purposes.  This research and its proposed device concept could be further developed to create better memory storage components, as well as to explore the potential of silicon's valley structure and spin interactions for efficient data processing.  It could also be utilized to provide a better understanding of the atomic compositions and crystalline structures that make up complex materials, and it provides a foundation for developing a range of innovative applications based on a wide range of materials. A $p_n$-division in the context of Euclidean geometry is equivalent to a particular type of configuration known as an $n$-simplex, whose facets meet at angles of $2/\pi$ or slightly sharper angles, depending on $n$ and the system's characteristics. To count these divisions, we employ a complementary approach, first estimating the total number of divisions and then applying the inclusion-exclusion principle to achieve the enumeration. A notable aspect of our findings is that all even-numbered dimensions greater than 2 enable the formation of $p_n$-divisions, whereas odd-numbered dimensions greater than 2 do not. This achievement is made possible by utilizing the geometric concept of a $p_n$-division and the inclusion-exclusion principle, which together allows us to derive an explicit formula for predicting the number of divisions in a space defined by a system of weights within an arbitrary dimension. This prediction is certain for all dimensions less than 4, and probable for all dimensions greater than 4. A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in identifying appropriate therapies to promote brain recovery and prevent further damage. Advanced treatments such as transcranial magnetic stimulation and cell-based therapies have shown promise but their effectiveness depends on accurate targeting of healthy brain areas around cerebral lesions. Since imaging techniques have limitations, we rely on mathematical models to accurately depict the lesions, yet determining the most accurate model parameter is difficult. To this end, we propose a novel framework for generating cerebral lesions based on a variational autoencoder, which enables us to navigate the trade-off between realistic lesion depiction and healthy brain surrounding, thus facilitating targeted treatments. The proposed method includes a progressive variational autoencoder that creates a compact representation of cerebral lesions, a discriminator ensuring spatial accuracy, and a controller for manipulating the model parameters, all integrated into a comprehensive model. Evaluating the model on publicly available datasets shows its superiority over existing methods, thus holding promise for guiding various therapies in stroke treatment. The code is available at: https://github.com/ghahramaniha/CerebralLesionGeneration.

However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. In order to accelerate the compilation of GP 2 programs, a new compiler extension for the GP 2 framework is introduced, which significantly boosts the performance of program verification tools using GP 2. The new compiler optimizes the conversion process for untyped graphs and enhances the capability to preserve shared variables in rooted rules. As a result, it provides a crucial performance improvement by reducing the examination depth required for rooted rules. To illustrate this key feature, a variant of the JML test case is presented, which demonstrates the capability of rooted rules to handle complex and recursive programs. The new compiler is also accompanied by a sample program verification task, which leverages rooted rules to ensure array references remain within specified bounds. In recent years, significant progress in deep learning has enabled high-performance image classification, but developing a universal feature extraction framework remains challenging. To address this, a new paradigm called comparative learning has emerged, which utilizes a comparison function to combine two views of data, often incorporating a contrastive loss to extract rich features. Building on this progress, this study further expands on comparative learning by introducing a unified structure that incorporates both inter compared and intra compared learning, resulting in the Unified Comparison Network (UCN). UCN has been successfully applied to various tasks, including inter compared learning with two classes and intra compared learning with multiple features, and has achieved superior performance in benchmark tests. The UCN model can be trained end-to-end using just a combination of the combination loss and the feature loss, and its simplicity, combined with flexible view configuration, make it a highly versatile tool for various feature extraction applications. The UCN code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ChenLiang162/UCN.

Working with nominal data poses specific challenges due to its ordinal nature. Despite this complication, many continuous relaxation methods have been successfully applied to nominal data. However, these methods often result in poor performance and interpretation issues. We demonstrate how a particular continuous relaxation approach, the Group Lasso, leads to undesirable outcomes when working with nominal data. For example, it can produce non-intuitive classification results or unnecessary dimension reduction. We argue that these negative consequences arise because the Group Lasso's quadratic penalty function contradicts the characteristics of nominal data. As such, we advise using a alternative relaxation method, such as the Group MC+ algorithm, designed specifically for ordinal data. In our experiments, we show how using Group MC+ leads to more practical and interpretable solutions when working with nominal data. One such application involves selecting relevant categories from a dataset with many nominal variables, a problem that is easily solved using Group MC+. In contrast, more complicated real-world examples, like a dataset with both nominal and continuous variables, require additional innovative strategies to solve. One approach involves using a combination of both Group MC+ and Lasso techniques, a method we demonstrate leads to accurate and interpretable results. Another example involves group classification problems, for which we use Group MC+ to develop a precise strategy, for both single-step and multi-step prediction processes. One note-worthy feature of Group MC+ involves its ability to handle continuous variables without any modification, as well as its compatibility with various regression techniques, for example, logistic regression. In our final experiment, we show how Group MC+ can be used to develop a decision-based classification method, for example, based on logistic regression, without the need for probability estimates. Rather, we use a threshold-based approach that is both simple and intuitive, for example, on datasets with both nominal and continuous variables. In summary, Group MC+ provides a flexible and adaptable framework for addressing complications arising from nominal data, as well as continuous variables, without any additional modifications. Despite this progress, the potential of these models has not been fully utilized for many applications, where structured knowledge is paramount, in areas such as information extraction from web pages, semantic search, and knowledge graph construction. One significant obstacle to their wider use is the lack of a clear method for incorporating structured knowledge into these models. In this work, we present a novel approach that integrates structured knowledge into LLMs through a technique called Knowledge Injection, demonstrating its benefits for both supervised and few-shot approaches. We apply this method to various tasks, showcasing the versatility of our approach. The research was conducted using a large web-based knowledge graph, making which is also a key contribution. We hope this work inspires further exploration into the many possibilities of incorporating structured knowledge into LLMs. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/ghaith/ability.

We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, labeled 1, 2, and 3, where systems 1 and 2 are uncorrelated with each other. We then examine the entanglement between systems 1 and 2 in relation to system 3's initial state, finding that the greatest entanglement between systems 1 and 2 occurs when system 3 is in a maximally mixed state, with the amount of entanglement directly proportional to the square of the coherence between system 3's initial state and the ground/state, as confirmed through both numerical and analytical methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this maximal entanglement can be achieved in a Jaynes-Cummings scenario, resulting in a controllable and sustainable level of entanglement between systems 1 and 2. The underlying dynamics are analyzed in detail, along with suggestions for real-world implementation using superconducting qubits. The significance of coherence's squared effect is broadly applicable, encompassing various entanglement-inducing paradigms based on Jaynes-Cummings interactions. The related thesis on coherent state generation completes the paper's content. The rising popularity of autonomous systems faces challenges due to the need for extensive training and potential safety constraints when learning from multiple agents observing the same environment. Typically, these agents are considered independent and individually provide labeled data for a learner, though in practice they often observe the same environment and can learn together. Our research proposes a novel framework, Co-Observer Learning, that combines the observation streams of agents without requiring an expert display of the underlying state. This framework assumes two agents with different observation streams learning separate policies, and we develop an appraoch to learn a single policy from their combined observation streams. Theoretical guarantees and effective algorithms are provided to ensure the learned policy is optimal under certain conditions. Experimental results show that co-observation learning together outperforms independent learning from the observation streams in various scenarios. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/ShuaiNiu-CoRL/Co-Observation Learning.

This paper introduces two key metrics for Randomized Advanced Encryption Standard (RAES) based Proxy Re-Encryption and Proxy Blind Signature schemes, which are necessary for constructing Valid Proxy Authenticated Encryption codes. We demonstrate the utility of these metrics by providing an algorithm to calculate the optimal probability of error (ERP) for PAC codes. Additionally, this paper shows that RAES-based RAES and RAES-based Proxy Blind Signature schemes have an acceptable ERP value, making them a viable substitute for standard AES in constrained systems. Furthermore, we discuss the implications for Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) security. The proposed algorithm was tested using the Mbed OS platform on several devices, including nRF52, ESP32, and MSP432. The results showed that the acceptable block length is low in a key space, however, in a large key space the optimal block length leads to performance comparable to standard AES. The paper also explores the possibility of reducing the key size further by deploying multi-round RAES-based PBTS schemes. The associated CoAP security protocol testing results are also presented. Evaluating the best action space size for reinforcement learning-based neural machine translation remains unclear, as both discrete word-level and action-probability-based approaches have their own limitations. A rigorous exploration of action space sizes reveals that larger spaces lead to performance degradation, contrary to common assumptions. To enhance translation quality, we reduce the action space by strategically selecting next actions, resulting in a significant 1.19 glossa word improvement over the baseline in the English-French translation task, and 1.05 glossa word improvement in the English-German context. Our method also demonstrates versatility when combined with different reinforcement learning objectives and threshold-based decoding methods. Our code has been made available at https://github.com/ghru/RL-NMT-action-space.

Researchers periodically apply and stop applying forces or energies to balance open quantum systems to study the behavior of systems driven by constant flows of energy and information. These systems, located between a heat source and a cold sink, reach a steady state where, on average, they neither gain nor lose energy or information. In a study involving a qubit driven by a periodic force, theorists have developed a precise theoretical description of its steady state. By comparing the results to experimental data from a superconducting qubit driven by a periodic signal, the accuracy of the theoretical model was validated, and the energy and information transfer rates between the qubit and its surroundings were determined precisely. Additionally, the system's responsiveness to forces and its connection to the cold sink or heating source were analyzed. This study's findings have significant implications for optimizing quantum systems driven by periodic signals and not equilibrium with their environments. Furthermore, by validating the theoretical model, this study provides a precise theoretical description of a widely studied, complex quantum system. Research on complex systems, which are resistant to destruction and able to thrive in challenging environments, involves uncovering the fundamental rules that these systems follow as they develop and evolve. A team of scientists from Russia, Germany, and the Netherlands has successfully applied a novel geometric approach to uncover hidden patterns in a particular magnetic nanoassemblies system. Through this method, known as Conformal Geometry Analysis, the researchers were able to uncover the assembly's precise geometric features by embedding it in a higher-dimensional space, effectively minimizing the distance between the assembly's perceived shape and its true, concealed form. By understanding this concealed geometry, the scientists were able to identify the locations and dynamics of defects within the assembly, such as misaligned magnetic fields, by mapping them onto the higher-dimensional space. In response to an external force, the assembly's concealed geometry allows us to predict how the defects will move and the assembly's structure will change, even remaking itself at the microscopic level through a process known as topological transition. This process, similar to the unfolding of a lotus flower, allows the assembly to regain its original configuration. The concealed geometry of this magnetic nanoassemblies system has significant implications for similar systems that exhibit pattern formation and possess robust and intricate structures, potentially allowing us to design and create such systems at the atomic level. In doing so, we may be able to transfer the principles underlying this system to other areas, including biology, where complex systems also thrive in challenging environments. A parametric family of generalized Hermite polynomials is introduced, which is subsequently linked to monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with potential $v$ in the complex plane. The potential $v$ has a finite number of poles and singularities, and its analytic properties are reflected in the generating function of the generalized Hermite polynomials. This connection enables the construction of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators with periodic potentials, as well as discrete ones. Furthermore, a transformation is derived that changes the number of poles in the potential, while maintaining the stability of the spectrum in the discrete case. Generalized Hermite polynomials also arise in the study of certain stochastic processes, specifically as the moments of the process's value, which, under certain conditions, can be interpreted as the expectation with respect to a measure that is equivalent to the Lebesgue measure. This leads to the application of these polynomials to establish the uniqueness of the invariant measure in the context of the stochastic Hermite-Hadamard inequality. This research was conducted in collaboration with M. Peche and S. Pétrés Hegyvари. The parameters of the generalized Hermite polynomials that are associated with the potential $v$ and the eigenfunction $\psi$ of the Schrödinger operator are linked through the Cauchy problem defined by the differential equation $\frac{dP}{dz} = 2(EP+F)$, where $E$ and $F$ are complex constants, that can be solved using the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula. The compatibility of this differential equation with the Schrödinger equation in the complex plane enables the derivation of a differential equation for the potential $v$, which can be solved to obtain the function $z \mapsto \theta(z)$ such that $v(z) = \theta(z) - \theta''(z)$. The fact that $\theta(z)$ is harmonic and determines the stability of the spectrum in the discrete case implies that the spectrum is controlled by the set of its zeros, which can be found using the Riemann-Hilbert problem. The method developed in this research paper can be applied to periodic and discrete potentials, as well as to the stochastic Hermite-Hadamard inequality, which leads to the application of generalized Hermite polynomials to the study of random matrices, specifically to the study of the spectrum of the Gaussian unitary ensemble. The paper concludes with the discussion of some open problems in this area.

Moreover, we establish that the representation theory of the extended Coxeter-Dynkin diagram $\widetilde{\Delta}$ contains information about the structure of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ through a relationship called the cluster-like property. This property is observable in the Hall-Littlewood series and character formulas for the irreducible representations of the extended Coxeter group $G(\widetilde{\Delta})$. Additionally, we provide a precise description of the irreducible representations of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ for specific Lie algebras $\mathfrak{g}$. Specifically, we cover the algebraic combinations associated with the cluster character of quantum groups, providing a graphical representation called Dynkin diagrams with nodes representing combinations, roots representing bonds between combinations, and tubes representing cluster operators. These diagrams serve as the foundation for classifying the invariant subcategories of the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{g})$ and determining the structure of the representation theory for a given Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. Furthermore, we include an introductory chapter on the fundamentals of cluster algebras, quantum groups, representation theory, and character theory. This chapter is designed to be accessible to students with basic knowledge in mathematics and physics. Lastly, we provide a concise overview of the paper's results along with some open questions and challenges in the concluding chapter. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive analysis of these schemes was previously unfeasible. However, the introduction of blockchain technology, which provides unprecedented transparency of transactions, now allows us to investigate the intricate structure of a prominent pyramid scheme known as Forsage. Through a detailed examination of Forsage, we reveal its intricate design, exposing the scams it facilitates and the financial gains of those behind it. The catalog of the Milky Way bulge's globular clusters remains a subject of debate. We investigated 19 candidate globular clusters within the bulge region using color-magnitude diagrams constructed from near-infrared photometry from the VVV survey. We determined the core radii, half-light radii, and radial profiles for these candidates by comparing observed star densities in the VVV survey fields. We also calculated the absolute magnitudes and horizontal hindgework points to distinguish between the candidates. We found that the core radii range from 0.56 to 5.05 arcseconds, the half-light radii range from 4.0 to 28.1 arcseconds, the absolute magnitudes in the V band range from -6.58 to -2.00, and the horizontal hindgework points in the VVV survey colors range from (4.56, 8.38) to (3.32, 7.17). We compared these characteristics to known globular clusters within the bulge to create a catalog of suspected cluster members by analyzing the radial profiles and color-magnitude diagrams. This research was primarily based on data from the VVV survey, with additional information derived from publicly available catalogs and databases, including the Catalog of Metallicity in Globular Clusters, the Harris catalog, and the 2MASS survey. We found that 13 of the 19 candidates have the necessary characteristics to be considered genuine globular clusters, with the remaining 6 awaiting further confirmation. These findings are consistent with the standard globular cluster parameter distributions, although 5 of the 13 confirmed clusters lie outside the typical bulge radius. These results highlight the difficulty of distinguishing real globular clusters from field stars within the bulge region based on photometric data alone and the importance of further surgical examination, such as spectroscopic analysis, to confirm the cluster membership of stars within these candidates. We also discuss the possible explanations for the 5 clusters that lie outside the standard bulge radius, including the presence of clusters in the bulge halo or the limitations of the current detection methods. These research findings highlight the value of the VVV survey in identifying new globular cluster candidates and the importance of further investigation into a few of the previously uncataloged clusters within the Milky Way bulge. We investigate key properties of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, specifically the characterizations they undergo via Fourier analysis. This leads to the examination of smoothness requirements for the continuity of certain operator norms. In particular, non-triviality conditions for the Gelfand-Shilov spaces $\Sigma^{\sigma}(\R^d)$ are established, along with characterizations involving Fourier transforms when these spaces contain analytic functions. These characterizations are further shown to be equivalent to the continuity of the operator norm of a class of Toeplitz operators, defined by their symbols within these spaces. This in turn is achieved via the study of the relationship between the operator norm and the $L^2$ norm of the operators in question, utilizing techniques from the properties of characterizing functions, specifically their smoothness and the behavior of their zeros. This research was conducted in collaboration with T. Ogawa. The results presented hereby are earlier known for the one-dimensional case ($d=1$). The contributions made in this paper are aimed at providing a generalization for the higher dimensional scenarios ($d \geq 2$). The characterizing Fourier transforms are also shown to be compatible with the change of variables formula, which in turn is equivalent to the compatibility with the change of variables in the context of the operator norm. This further leads to the derivation of the conditions under which the operator norms of the Toeplitz operators are invariant with respect to the changes of variables. The results obtained hereby are a generalization of the results presented in the paper by T. Ogawa for the one-dimensional case ($d=1$). Understanding and generating point clouds have broad applications in computer vision. Despite the success of graph-based models in processing point clouds, current neural network architectures face challenges in setting valid sampling probabilities to match real-world data distributions. Existing methods employ arbitrary probability schedules that may hinder the convergence to accurate data distributions. A novel neural network called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPS) addresses this issue by designing a stochastic optimizer that guarantees convergence to a specific data distribution unique to the transformation used. Experimental results on three datasets demonstrate that TPS yields superior performance compared to conventional baselines, specifically in generating realistic point clouds under complex transformations and strict density constraints. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghj121/TPS.

In this work, we introduce a new clustering method called Influence-Based Graph Clustering (IBGC) specifically designed for dynamical systems modeled on networks. These models comprise nodes representing variables and directed edges representing the causal relationships between these variables. The approach we present focuses on identifying subnetworks where the variables are consistently changed in the same direction throughout time. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed rules to determine the orientation of causal relationships, IBGC utilizes data to determine these connections. Furthermore, in contrast to conventional methods that prioritize connecting existing clusters over time, our approach prioritizes the change in the network's state over time. We have tested IBGC on synthetic and real-world data, revealing its effectiveness in detecting changes and identifying meaningful clusters in networks compared to current methods. Generative adversarial networks (GANs) aim to synthesize authentic data by pitting two opposing neural networks against each other. In standard GAN training, both components learn and improve simultaneously. We've developed SparseGAN, a novel framework that separates training for both networks, assigning separate datasets for each to learn from. This approach yields more effective and efficient learning for both components. We've also introduced the Adversarial Training Network (ATN) variant, which generates a single, usable sample during training. Both SparseGAN and ATN variants outperform current state-of-the-art methods in various datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR10, and VGGFace. Additionally, we've applied this approach to text generation, obtaining a new benchmark for the Large Language Model, LLAMA. Code has been made publicly available on SparseGAN GitHub repository.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another through panspermia, potentially including interstellar routes, is both intriguing and useful for extending the scope of habitability studies. We examine the likelihood of interstellar panspermia and related microbial survival scenarios, considering the various factors that affect it, such as the duration of journey time, how microbes respond to space environment, the impact of cosmic radiation, and the effectiveness of transfer mechanisms between planets and within planetary systems. We also investigate the potential for interstellar panspermia to succeed in various scenarios, such as between specific star systems, in different types of stellar environments, and during designated time periods. By better understanding the viability of interstellar panspermia, we can identify the conditions that support the transfer of life and contribute to the development of a framework for evaluating microbial transfer and the dissemination of life in the astrophysical context, and therefore the diversity of possible biosignatures, particularly those related to exoplanetary surface environments. We present data on projected time spans for various microbial survival scenarios in space, as well as forecasts for systems that could support interstellar panspermia in the near future, based on current exoplanetary detection techniques and future astronomical surveys. We find that planets orbiting low mass stars, once they become habitable, could succeed in transferring life between them with a high probability over extended periods, and that areas associated with recent star formation show a higher potential for biogenic signals related to surface environments. We discuss the scope of these findings for various contexts, including the detection of life, the transfer of life, and the possibility of biotic environments in the universe. We conclude by analyzing the relationships between distributive processes of life, its transfer, and its dissemination in the universe, with potential applications to evaluating recurring planets and the cosmic origins of life. Animal population studies often rely on capture-recapture data, where individuals are captured and identified multiple times, and abundance estimates are derived from these data. Another approach to studying animal populations involves selected locations that animals choose from a wider set of possible sites, with abundance inferences based on the chosen locations. Although these methods can be used separately to estimate population abundance, their individual limitations can result in inaccurate estimates. Our study combines capture-recapture data from specific sites with selected locations chosen by the animals, using a Bayesian approach to analyze the capture-recapture data and another Bayesian approach to analyze the selected locations, and incorporates the two analyses to make inferences about the population abundance. We tested this combined method on simulated data and found it outperformed the separate capture-recapture analysis alone. Additionally, this method allows for inferences about population abundance, migration rates, and the spatial distribution of animals, and provides a method for estimating the detection probability that is independent of capture-recapture data. Our research also highlights potential applications to studies involving selected locations across a larger area, such as camera trap surveys, with animals choosing to visit certain locations from a wider set of possible sites. Our analysis of these methods also touches on the relationship between the availability of capture-recapture data at different sites and the accuracy of the combined analysis, which can inform the design of future studies involving selected locations. Our method, known as ``SCR-REDS'', is available online for public use. We evaluated this method using capture-recapture data from animal studies in the wild, including turtles, alligators, and songbirds, which allowed us to estimate the accuracy of the method and identify areas for methodological improvement. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a higher level of accuracy than single-layer networks. However, the transmission of signals between layers is not well understood and requires further investigation. In this study, we focus on multilayer networks and examine the transmission of solutions between oscillators in different layers. Our analysis reveals that the transmission of signals can take various forms, including blocking, partial transmission, and exact replication, depending on the specific conditions meets. We have also derived a new multilayer complex network model, which can be simplified to a single-layer network when the transmission of signals between oscillators in different layers does not replicate exactly. This new model provides a more accurate representation of certain dynamic systems than traditional single-layer models. Furthermore, we have investigated the transmission of solutions in multilayer networks with layer overlap, discovering that the transmission of signals between oscillators in different layers can result in the creation of new isolated components and affect the stability of the system. Our research has implications for a range of fields, including neuroscience, economics, and climate science, where the importance of signal transmission between different components is well documented. We have also made our results available in the form of an interactive dashboard that enables users to explore our findings graphically. This study can serve as a foundation for future investigations into the complex dynamics of multilayer networks. Our code is available for download upon request. The methodology used in this study is applicable to a wide range of multilayer network models, including those with directed connections and weighted edges. Finally, we have identified potential future research avenues in this area. Given a field $K$ containing a finite subset $S$ as its subfield, and a quadratic extension $L$ of $K$ with the basis $\{1,\omega\}$, we define the set $V_S$ consisting of vector trajectories that can be expressed as products of the form $f(t) \cdot g(t)\omega$, where $f$ and $g$ are elements from the extension field $L$. We identify the field structures associated with $V_S$, specifically for the fields related to the algebraic extensions $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3})$ and $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{5})$. Additionally, we determine the conditions under which the set $V_S$ forms a field for the general case. By examining the recorded data, we were able to identify distinct patterns of activity associated with walking steps in both groups. Furthermore, our analysis revealed that the ECoG activity pattern occurred immediately before the sound of each stepping rhythm, suggesting a direct link between the activity and rhythmic neural processes. Identifying complex relationships within time-dependent data sets is a challenging task that can benefit from advanced neural network techniques. In this work, we develop a novel connection detection framework, known as DEDICATE, which discovers dynamic connections within multivariate time series data using graph neural networks. We demonstrate that DEDICATE effectively extracts both linear and nonlinear connections across different time scales, and that the method's effectiveness is comparable to that of state-of-the-art methods in multiple scenarios. Additionally, we apply DEDICATE to the analysis of a numerical example, a biological network, and real-world financial and physiological data, in order to gain insights into its capabilities. Our findings show that DEDICATE is a versatile and powerful tool with a wide range of potential applications in fields such as physics, biology, finance, and medicine. Our code is available at https://github.com/yong024/DEDICATE.

Animals play a significant role in various ecological processes, requiring their geographical tracks to be identified and analyzed. While camera traps provide a vast amount of footage containing potential footage of animals in their natural habitat, manually sifting through the content to extract movement from still images and identify moving objects within videos is a significant challenge. This task is even more complex for humans due to the abundance of irrelevant content, including stationary animals, making it necessary to develop a robust and automatic method to detect biologic movement in videos. In this research, we develop a novel approach to tackle this issue by creating a dataset that can be used to train models and demonstrate our proposed approach's effectiveness. Our method has potential applications in various fields beyond biological movement detection, in areas such as video surveillance, film industry, and video compression. We have also incorporated motion into the existing video analysis framework, presenting a novel approach to estimate a score that represents the level of movement in each frame. This score can be visually embedded back into the video or used for various purposes, offering a high level of practical value. We have tested and validated our method, presenting multiple case studies and comparing it to existing approaches, also exploring possible improvements to our model. Our code is available for public use on GitHub. Networks with random defects can convey information reliably, maintaining integrity in the presence of disorder, by leveraging topological characteristics. These topological robustness properties have been demonstrated in 2D networks with a single type of random defect, yet the underlying physics for networks containing two types of random defects is not well understood. In this study, we examine a 2D topological conductor with random binary imperfections, representing it as a tight-binding model. Our findings show that this model exhibits both bulk topological characteristics and marginally topological behavior, resulting in the emergence of zero-energy edge states and protected pockets in the energy spectrum. These features are made possible by the interplay between two types of random defects, which create unique environments that are insensitive to the disorder. We propose that such networks can be created using carbon-based materials, and suggest an experimental design for a graphene-based topological conductor. Furthermore, we predict that incorporating impurities can lead to the appearance of zero-voltage gaps and topological phase transitions induced by tuning the randomness of the network. Our calculations indicate that adjusting the amount of disorder can shift the network from a topological phase characterized by edge states, to an non-topological phase with a gap, providing a theoretical basis for a novel concept called Topological Anderson Switches. The complex interaction between two types of random defects in networks also leads to non-trivial effects on the edge states and topological characteristics, ranging from the creation of topological defects and boundaries, to interactions with crystallographic features of the network. The unique properties of these networks, coupled with potential experimental implementations, make them ideal candidates for realizing novel topological devices, such as Topological Anderson Conductors and Topological Anderson Switches. The discovery of edge states and topological characteristics in a 2D network with random binary imperfections opens a new chapter in the study of topological robustness, presenting both theoretical and experimental challenges that can lead to groundbreaking innovations in the field of topological materials. The underlying physics for networks containing two types of random defects also provides theoretical evidence that supports experimental findings of edge states in Silylene-based pi-systems, and predicts similar behavior in other materials, such as Quinacene-based pi-systems. Contextual decision-making is a challenging task that involves combining contextual information, which is often local to agents, and their private parameters to make informed decisions. In a recent study, a conceptual framework known as contextual linear gambits has been introduced to efficiently learn contextual decisions through observation of others' actions and outcomes. Within this framework, multiple contextual linear gambits have been considered, where each agent has a separate parameter for their contextual model. By observing others' actions and receiving feedback on those actions, agents can update their contextual models without exchanging contextual information. However, existing algorithms in this framework assume that the number of contexts is known in advance, which can be difficult to determine often. In response, a new learning algorithm is proposed for a specific instance of multiple contextual linear gambits, known as the multi-agent linear contextual regret matching algorithm, which is able to estimate the number of contexts and learn the contextual model without knowing the number of contexts. Through theoretical analysis and simulation studies, the proposed algorithm is shown to converge to a pure strategy equilibrium and outperforms existing alternatives when the number of contexts is unknown. Which is proven through an increase in regret bounded by a constant factor. In addition, a new challenge known as the contextual overfitting problem is identified, which can result in the agent learning an inaccurate contextual model, especially when the number of contexts is large. To address this issue, a new algorithm is developed which is robust against contextual overfitting and learns a contextual model that is equivalent to the maximum likelihood estimator. Which is proven through statistical analysis. In addition, simulation studies demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through comparison with alternative learning algorithms in a variety of scenarios. Which includes scenarios with both known and unknown numbers of contexts, as well as scenarios with high-dimensional contextual models. Which can result in large numbers of contexts. In addition, a new theoretical result known as the contextual regret bound is proven, which provides a bound on the regret of the proposed algorithm. Our research involves examining the underlying assumptions of QGP properties in heavy-ion collisions, specifically focusing on the initial conditions that shape final collision results. To achieve this, we investigated four distinct event amplitude configurations in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy using the ALICE detector and the AMPT model. Our analysis evaluated charged particle spectra and elliptic flow patterns to determine how they are influenced by initial condition characteristics, including the size and shape of collision events. Our study revealed that initial condition configurations that produce larger, more circular amplitudes tend to result in higher short-range collectivity, while those with more asymmetric shapes exhibit longer-range collectivity. Furthermore, we found that initial condition configurations that produce larger, more circular amplitudes lead to higher long-range collectivity in low-transverse-velocity regions. Our findings highlight the complex interplay between the collectivity of a system and the shape of that system, demonstrating how collections of particles that reside in the outer regions of the collision area primarily contribute to long-range collectivity, and that initial condition configurations that prioritize middle- and forward-collosion region size tend to result in higher collectivity. Our research also illustrates how event amplitude configurations that prioritize middle-collosion region size over forward-collosion region size delay the onset of long-range collectivity, in addition to providing further insights into initial condition characteristics, final-state collectivity, and charged particle distributions. Our study identified potential misinterpretation of collected data, given that the assumed assumption of constant initial charge density may need adjustment, given that charge density is influenced by the size of the collision event, specifically in the middle-collosion region. Moreover, our analysis discovered that the assumed assumption of constant initial geometry may need adjustment, given that collision event shapes affect long-range collectivity, charged particle distributions, and final-state collectivity, ultimately suggesting that initial condition characteristics should be determined through data analysis rather than theoretical assumption. This study introduces an innovative integration approach for simulating multiple steps of a particle collision, allowing for greater flexibility in modeling collisions in dyadic simulations. Unlike current methods that treat collisions instantaneously, this model takes into account the physical duration of collisions, capturing crucial information in each time step. A statistical analysis of collision data from particle simulations with different time step integrations reveals that shorter time steps generally result in more accurate collisions, but at the cost of slower simulation speeds. As such, this study aims to optimize time step integration to balance simulation efficiency and collision accuracy while accounting for the effects of surface roughness and particle anisotropy. A comparative assessment of four different integration approaches evaluates their effectiveness in simulating collisions and retaining the accuracy of results, ultimately identifying a preferred method for reducing simulation errors and increasing speed. By modifying the collision time step based on the local flow conditions, this study also introduces a novel multi-time-step integration approach that further enhances simulation accuracy and allows for a greater range of applicable time steps. A numerical simulation of a particle colliding with a flat wall demonstrates the physical significance of capturing the duration of collisions, while a statistical analysis of collision time steps in real-world applications highlights the broad applicability of this method across various scenarios. A public repository is available for this study, along with examples of simulations that illustrate the physical implications of collision duration and surface roughness on particle collisions. Moreover, this binding statement indirectly supports the unproved conjecture of Albert and Lewis, which asserts that all positive integers forming the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ must be powers of a specific prime number, in this case $7$. This research focuses on advancing the design of a monopod for hopping on soft, uneven ground by conducting simulations and improving the initial design. The aim is to explore the feasibility of a monopod for hazardous terrains considered off-limits for traditional four-legged robots. The soft environment was simulated using a finite element method, and the impact on the ground was assessed using a factor critical to ensuring safety around human assets. To enhance the design, modifications were made, and these changes were validated through physical experiments. The monopod's hopping pattern was also altered to minimize the impact radius, and a successful reduction of 45% in the area affected was demonstrated. Furthermore, a control strategy was developed to accommodate unexpected soft ground, resulting in a successful hike through a scenario mimicking such conditions. The system's versatility was proven by transferring the design to a different terrain and successfully adapting to it. While existing research focuses on specific tiny substructures like triangles and clusters, a more comprehensive approach is needed to extract a wide variety of structures, as desired patterns can vary greatly in size, shape, and complexity. Currently, algorithms are largely inflexible and cannot adapt to the unique characteristics of information networks, which are quite diverse. A new approach called Structure Discovery Engine (SDE) addresses this limitation by enabling automatic formation of customized patterns and optimizing a range of objective functions that reflect the significance of discovered structures. SDE also integrates multiple data sources and represents the resulting patterns using a semantic web framework that facilitates easy integration with existing systems and smooth transition to a dynamic graph representation. In contrast to static frameworks, SDE provides extensive opportunities for user input that cater to the ever-changing nature of information networks. Our case studies on Wikipedia and LinkedIn networks demonstrate the versatility and effectiveness of SDE. Furthermore, SDE is distinct from similar approaches in that it offers an open architecture that allows effortless substitution of different algorithms and easy integration with other systems, along with a user-friendly interface that allows for easy input of parameters and patterns. The source code of SDE is available at https://github.com/yashkw/StructureDiscoveryEngine. Quantum annealing within a suitable interval can lead to successful outcomes, however, the beginning of this interval is not clear.  This study demonstrates that by comparing classical and quantum dynamics, we can identify the starting point of the quantum annealing schedule, which becomes evident through the relation of action gap and barrier height in a simple Ising model.  As a result, successful quantum failure is achieved in the majority of simulations for the exact cover issue.  In particular, when the number of qubits represents a prime number, the quantum annealing interval reduces to nothing, and this condition is found to be crucial for understanding the effect of prime numbers on successful outcomes.  Interestingly, outside the quantum annealing interval, quantum dynamics can suddenly change to exponential decay driven by the barrier height.  This finding is further confirmed by means of classical simulation, where the action gap obtained agrees with the results of quantum annealing.  Finally, the study of prime numbers is extended to the scenario of multiple islands of successful outcomes, where it is discovered that the introduction of an error threshold can help in the transition between the islands, and this situation differs significantly from the scenario of random errors.  In particular, the situation with multiple islands of successful outcomes represents a complex, chaotic regime, where the fluctuation of global parameters across the islands leads to a random alteration among the islands, and this situation is in sharp contrast to the random alteration among the qubit strings, which occurs in the absence of an error threshold.  The research was conducted using a conventional D-Wave quantum annealer and classical simulated annealing, and the results were verified through two independent approaches of simulation, which include the quantum annealing simulation itself, and the classical simulated annealing simulation.  The findings of the study were applied to a real-world problem of genome assembly, and the outcome showed that the approach of the study is effective for complex problems that involve multiple islands of successful outcomes.  The study also discovered that the transition from quantum survival to quantum failure is driven by a sudden change in the dynamics from a state of stable chaos to an state of unstable chaos, which occurs outside the quantum annealing interval, and this situation differs significantly from the exponential decay driven by the barrier height, which occurs in the scenario of single island of successful outcomes.  The finding of the study about the relation of prime numbers to complex problems that involve multiple islands of successful outcomes is novel, and it has not been reported before. Our study examines the challenge of achieving high-temperature stability in correlated oxides with a d-orbital arrangement, specifically focusing on nickelate materials. To better understand this challenge, we investigated a dual-band model with strong interaction and screening effects, simulating a (110) plane-oriented nickelate substrate. Screening interactions were found to be extremely difficult to overcome, as they result in the formation of an internal barrier within the orbital arrangement. Furthermore, a slight displacement of the oxygen planes from the (110) orientation was found to significantly impact the number of bands and their energy levels, offers potential strategies for enhancing stability, and provides a framework for identifying suitable materials with a single-band scenario. Lastly, a comparison with cuprate materials reveals a unique feature of the nickelate model, namely that the energy gap closes when the oxygen displacement exceeds half a lattice spacing, potentially allowing for metallic behavior in these materials. The screening model also exhibits reliable resilience in the face of temperature increases and vibrational perturbations, offering a promising future research direction in which the oxygen planes are slightly displaced, a feature that could be experimentally realized through the manipulation of the nickelate substrate. The underlying physics of this challenge are so fundamental that they result in the screening of both the direct and exchange interactions, requiring a dual-band perspective in a local orbital arrangement, and demonstrating how easy it is to mistakenly interpret the metallic behavior of these materials, a difficulty that presents itself in both nickelate and other, similar materials like cobaltate and Ta-doped strontium ruthenate. The study concludes by highlighting the dual-band nature of these materials, the difficulties of screening interaction in a local orbital arrangement, and the straightforward experimental normalization of oxygen displacement, making this research applicable to a broad range of materials beyond just nickelate. The structure and stability of dense stellar matter are scrutinized within dense stellar matter, which contains strange quark matter, using a model where the quark interaction includes a complex diquark correlation.  Despite the complexity of this model, its equation of state can be effectively represented by simpler models, which are widely studied.  However, our analysis indicates that the original model cannot be accurately mimicked by the commonly used relativistic mean-field diquark-antidiquark interaction model, particularly in high density regimes.  Consequently, dense stellar matter that consists of strange quarks may possess a critical density above which it loses stability, ranging from 4 to 8 times nuclear saturation density, with masses of strange quark stars potentially ranging from 0.8 to 1.2 times the Chandrasekhar limit.  This could be a possible explanation for the observed upper limit on neutron star mass, and is relevant for future studies of compact stars motivated by the strong evidence for matter with strangeness found in heavy ion collisions and astronomical observations.  Our analysis highlights the significance of treating diquark correlations correctly when studying the properties of dense stellar matter, and underlines the potential for four-quark states in high-density environments.
